reference.source: Fitzpatrick's Dermatology / Rook's Textbook of Dermatology
clinicalPearls: Erythroderma is defined as erythema and scaling affecting more than about 90 per cent of the body surface, and is a clinical syndrome rather than a single disease
The most frequent underlying causes are pre-existing dermatoses (psoriasis, atopic and other eczemas), drug reactions, and cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, with a proportion remaining idiopathic
Always take a careful history of prior skin disease and recent drug exposures, as these often reveal the trigger
Look for diagnostic clues within the redness: nail and scalp changes suggesting psoriasis, lymphadenopathy raising concern for lymphoma, or an eruption temporally linked to a new medication
Widespread skin failure impairs thermoregulation, fluid balance, and the barrier against infection, so treat these patients as systemically unwell
Management centres on supportive care (warmth, fluids, emollients, nutrition) alongside identification and treatment of the underlying cause and withdrawal of any culprit drug
Repeated skin biopsies over time may be needed because early histology is frequently non-specific and the cause can declare itself later
Beware secondary infection and consider it in any patient who deteriorates or develops systemic upset
reference.pathophysiology: Erythroderma reflects a massive inflammatory response in the skin, whatever the trigger, with markedly increased epidermal turnover and a dense dermal inflammatory infiltrate producing generalised erythema and scaling. Loss of the intact cutaneous barrier over almost the entire surface leads to substantial transepidermal water loss, protein and heat loss, and high cutaneous blood flow. The resulting physiological derangements include impaired temperature regulation, fluid and electrolyte disturbance, hypoalbuminaemia, and high-output cardiac demand. The specific microscopic pattern depends on the underlying disease, which is why histology and clinical correlation are both required.
additionalDifferentials: Atopic or other eczema progressing to erythroderma
Inherited ichthyoses and pemphigus foliaceus in specific settings
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy, often repeated, to help identify the underlying dermatosis
Peripheral blood film and flow cytometry to look for circulating atypical (Sezary) cells
Bloods assessing fluid, electrolyte, albumin, and infection status
Drug history review and consideration of eosinophilia and organ involvement suggesting DRESS
Cultures if secondary infection or sepsis is suspected
redFlags: Dermatological emergency: extensive skin failure causes impaired thermoregulation and a high-output cardiac state requiring urgent supportive management
Fluid, electrolyte, and protein loss leading to dehydration, hypotension, and metabolic derangement
Secondary bacterial infection or sepsis complicating the compromised barrier
Features suggesting DRESS or an evolving lymphoma requiring specialist input
Frail, elderly, or comorbid patients in whom cardiovascular decompensation is more likely
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends heavily on the underlying cause and the patient's comorbidities; many drug-related and dermatosis-related cases resolve with treatment, but lymphoma-associated and idiopathic erythroderma may run a protracted or relapsing course, and severe cases carry meaningful morbidity and mortality.
pitfalls: Focusing on the skin alone and neglecting fluid balance, temperature, and nutritional support
Assuming a single early biopsy excludes lymphoma or a specific dermatosis
Failing to identify and stop a causative drug
Underestimating the cardiovascular strain of high cutaneous blood flow in older patients
Missing secondary infection as a cause of clinical deterioration
management: Treat as systemically unwell with admission and supportive care: maintain warmth, correct fluid and electrolyte disturbance, provide nutritional support, and apply liberal emollients and bland topical therapy to restore the barrier
Identification and treatment of the underlying cause, with immediate withdrawal of any culprit drug
Disease-specific therapy directed at the trigger, using systemic agents for psoriasis or eczema, and phototherapy or chemotherapy for cutaneous T-cell lymphoma
Systemic corticosteroids for drug-related causes such as DRESS, avoiding them in psoriasis where they may precipitate deterioration
Active monitoring for and treatment of complications including secondary skin infection and sepsis, hypothermia, hypoalbuminaemia and high-output cardiac failure
Skin biopsy, often repeated, with peripheral blood film and flow cytometry to identify the underlying dermatosis or Sezary cells
Dermatology-led multidisciplinary care with high-dependency support for severe cases
